title: The hypertrophy series: the importance of going to failure for muscle building
summary: He defines 'going to failure' as stopping one rep short of actually failing, and argues bodybuilders should reach muscular failure on every working set. Failure must be balanced across heavy and moderate rep ranges, and he lists his preferred rep ranges for it.

claims.claim: Going to failure is not failing: it means stopping one rep short of a missed rep.
An actual missed rep (bar on chest, bailing a squat, dropping a deadlift) is a miscalculation in your programme; it shouldn't happen when training for size, though it may be part of powerlifting.
Going to failure puts you at 100% of the intensity range; the next rep would be the one you fail. You should reach the top of that range on every set.
In his view there's no point not going to failure, since stopping short means you stop before maximal muscular damage.
Mechanical failure (e.g. thoracic spine rounding on a squat until the bar falls) is not muscular failure and doesn't count as lifting to failure.
Reaching muscular failure on every working set is the bodybuilder's goal; good technique lets you max out muscular endurance before cardio or mechanics stop you.
He doesn't define hard sets versus easy sets by failure; to him going to failure is a given on working sets.
Going to failure is repeatable and isn't the same as burning out; recovery time and injury risk depend on the load used when you reach failure.
Failure on a 2-rep-max deadlift taxes the body completely differently from failure on deficit deadlifts for 8-12 reps.
Always going to failure on very heavy lifts is unbalanced, and so is always going to failure on light high-rep work; combine strength work with variation and accessory work.
If you take a set of 12 to failure you should still get at least 8 reps on the next set, unless you hyped yourself up artificially for the first set.
Going to failure lets rep counts fall naturally across sets, and combined with evolving rep ranges this gives steady volume progression and more tonnage over time.
Very high-rep sets are a poor fit for going to failure because cardiovascular or mechanical failure arrives before muscular failure.
His preferred rep ranges for going to failure: 2-5, 4-8, 6-10, 8-12 and 12-15.
